problem: The units are given wrongly: s is in kJ/(kg·K) but u and h are in kJ/kg, not kJ/kg K. Writing 'use s, u, h in kJ/kg K' tells students that enthalpy and internal energy carry a per-kelvin unit, which is false and will cost marks in the exam.
fix: Use s, u, h in kJ/kg K only if you want specific values in kJ/kg. Replace with: A and G are totals in kJ; the specific functions are a = u − Ts and g = h − Ts, in kJ/kg, with u and h in kJ/kg and s in kJ/(kg·K).

problem: 'Both functions are unchanged, as they must be' overstates the case. At a phase change at equilibrium temperature and pressure only ΔG is exactly zero; in general ΔA = −pΔV at constant T and p, so it is zero here only because the volume change of freezing water is negligible.
fix: Step 6: ΔG is exactly zero for a phase change at its equilibrium temperature and pressure. ΔA is zero here only because the volume change is negligible; in general ΔA = −pΔV, which is small but not zero.

where: Section 3, last paragraph of the bullet list
problem: A turbine shaft is not a constant-temperature, constant-pressure device; a real turbine is adiabatic and its shaft work is bounded by the change in availability (exergy), not by −ΔG. Listing it next to a battery and a fuel cell may confuse the condition under which −ΔG is the bound.
fix: A battery, a fuel cell, an electrolyser: the non-pV work they deliver or absorb at constant T and p is bounded by −ΔG. A steady-flow device such as a turbine at constant T and p has the same bound on shaft work.
